content: To ensure the elimination of measles is sustained and to prevent the re-establishment of endemic measles virus transmission, countries and regions must continue implementing the strategies that were initially used to achieve elimination. These strategies include: 1. Achieving and maintaining high vaccination coverage: It is critical to sustain a vaccination coverage rate of at least 95% with two doses of measles-containing vaccine (MCV) through routine immunization programs. Supplementary immunization activities (SIAs) should be conducted when necessary to address immunity gaps. 2. Conducting high-quality case-based measles surveillance: Surveillance systems must be robust and capable of identifying and classifying suspected measles cases accurately. This includes timely reporting and investigation of cases. 3. Ensuring high-quality laboratory support for surveillance: Accredited laboratories must provide timely and accurate testing of samples to confirm or discard suspected measles cases. These laboratories should also be capable of detecting measles virus for genotyping and molecular analysis to monitor virus transmission patterns. 4. Developing and maintaining outbreak preparedness and response capabilities: Countries must be prepared to respond rapidly to measles outbreaks. This includes managing cases effectively and implementing control measures to prevent further spread. Governments, with the assistance of National Verification Committees (NVCs) or Sub-Regional Verification Committees (SRVCs), should conduct annual assessments of their progress in maintaining measles elimination. Annual progress reports should be submitted to the Regional Verification Commission (RVC). The RVC will review these reports, conduct field visits when necessary, and provide feedback and recommendations to governments through the NVCs or SRVCs. Verification of Measles Elimination Countries must document their measles elimination status, including: The history of measles elimination efforts. Incidence and epidemiology of measles cases. Virus detection and identification data. Performance of epidemiologic and laboratory surveillance systems. Immunity profiles of the population. Sustainability of elimination efforts. Risks to Measles Elimination Countries should identify and address risks that could jeopardize the achievement or maintenance of measles elimination. These risks include: Inadequate population immunity. Insufficient surveillance to detect and classify imported, import-related, or endemic transmission. Gaps in outbreak preparedness and response. Current and Proposed Plans Countries should outline their current and proposed plans for measles elimination, including: Strategies to improve population immunity. Enhancements to epidemiologic and virologic surveillance systems. Preparedness and response plans for outbreaks. Verification processes to confirm elimination status. Immunization Coverage and Surveillance Indicators Countries must monitor key indicators, such as: Routine immunization coverage rates for MCV1 and MCV2. SIA coverage rates. Proportion of suspected cases with adequate investigation and blood specimen collection. Laboratory performance, including the timeliness of results and virus detection capabilities. Sustainability Countries should ensure that measles elimination activities are integrated into national health plans and budgets. This includes securing sufficient funding for routine immunization and outbreak response activities. Governments and donors must commit to addressing funding gaps to sustain elimination efforts. Challenges Challenges to achieving and sustaining measles elimination include: Maintaining high vaccination coverage. Ensuring sensitive and representative surveillance systems. Responding effectively to outbreaks. Addressing other systemic issues that may hinder elimination efforts. Action Plan for 2013 and Beyond Countries should develop detailed action plans to achieve and sustain measles elimination. These plans should include specific activities, expected outcomes, timeframes, budgets, and funding sources. Monitoring and evaluation mechanisms should be established to track progress and address gaps. By adhering to these strategies and recommendations, countries can ensure the long-term success of measles elimination efforts and protect their populations from this preventable disease.
